messages.content: You are an expert space systems engineer providing detailed technical specifications.

You are an expert space systems engineer for Project Dyson, a non-profit
planning the construction of a Dyson swarm.

Provide a DETAILED technical proposal for: **Mining Robots**
Context: Phase 0 - Space Resource Processing

## Phase 0 after the 2026 re-assessment (binding context)

The original Phase 0 plan (a central 50 kt/yr processing station at Sun–Earth L4/L5, crew visits,
production LOX/LH₂, 100 kW-class freighters) was found not to close and is abandoned. Design for the
revised architecture below. Do not re-propose the abandoned design.

### Agreed by all three re-assessment models
- Split Phase 0 into 0A (research + pathfinders) and gated 0B (industrial): Structure agreed; budgets → §3 (All three)
- Abandon 50 kt/yr central SEL4/L5 ore processing: — (All three)
- Co-locate at least beneficiation and primary processing at the target NEA; ship product, not ore: Reference architecture (All three. GPT: "favoured but not universally optimal". Claude retains a central station fed with ≥20:1 concentrate as an alternative. Gemini's own weighted QOC scores SEL1 marginally higher (see §6).)
- Narrow product to native/reduced Fe-Ni; defer solar-grade Si and oxide-derived Al/Si: Fe-Ni baseline; Al/Si pilot or deferred (All three)
- Delivered product scale of order 1 kt/yr: 0.6–2.5 kt/yr (Claude 0.6–2.2 (central 1.3); Gemini 1.0–2.5 (1.5, of which 0.3 is water); GPT 0.6–1.0 contracted (0.67–1.33 capacity))
- MW-class cargo tugs: 1.0–2.5 MWe each; 10–18 tugs; 150–300 t payload (→ §3 for point values)
- Robots powered by HV tether from site power, with onboard battery for mobility and safe-mode: 1–3 kV; battery 10–50 kWh (Claude 2–3 kV, 10–30 kWh; Gemini 1–3 kV, 15–25 kWh; GPT 20–50 kWh, voltage unspecified)
- Delete the 200–500 MWh Li-ion line; size storage per site: 0.5–15 MWh total (Claude 0.5–3 MWh + thermal; GPT 1.3–3.3 MWh; Gemini <15 MWh (YAML 10 MWh))
- Reject $5/W array pricing: Hardware ~$30–150/W, launch separately accounted (Claude $30–150/W hardware ($50–230 installed incl. launch); Gemini $60–100/W (spec $75, range $50–110); GPT $30–100/W allowance ($45–220 with delivery))
- Replace 32–50 × 100 kg monoprop prospectors: Remote survey + 4–10 EP rendezvous scouts of 200–600 kg (All three agree a monoprop bus has ~0.5–0.8 km/s Δv. Remote-survey method differs (→ §3).)
- Add an Earth-to-space launch/delivery line: Line agreed; magnitude → §3 (All three)
- Add a comms, ground segment and mission-operations line; DSN not assumed free: Line agreed (All three. Claude and GPT reject the round-1 2.5 TB/day (~230 Mbps) figure.)
- Phase 0 uncrewed; remove habitat and quarterly visits: 0 crew visits (All three. Claude and GPT reject the "human-rating" label in favour of structural reserve plus docking/servicing interfaces. Gemini keeps docking ports and structural margins without commenting on the label.)
- Add an EP propellant supply line; xenon not baselined: Line agreed; demand → §3 (All three)
- No production LOX/LH₂ in Phase 0: — (All three. Claude and GPT remove the EML1 depot; Gemini "defers" cryo depots to 0B/Phase 1.)
- Add NRE, pathfinder, spares and contingency lines: Lines agreed; values → §3 (All three)
- Write a full organization (bom-0-7) specification: ~$100–350M (Claude $100–300M; Gemini $150–250M (text $200M); GPT $150–350M)
- Add a debris/contamination requirement and budget tighter than 99%: $50–300M (Threshold → §3)
- Freeze one configuration-controlled baseline; mark legacy documents superseded: — (All three)
- Earth-supplied material as a fallback if microgravity metallurgy fails: — (All three. Ranking relative to lunar → §3.)
- Tie Phase 0 output to Phase 1 demand with a material/purity/date specification: — (All three)
- Add waste-heat rejection (radiators) explicitly: Item agreed; sizing → §3 (All three)

### Owner decisions
- D-01 (accepted 2026-10-12): Fund 0A. Hold 0B as a gated real option, sized at the gate by signed Phase 1 demand. Call Phase 0 a capability programme, not a cost saving.
- D-02 (accepted 2026-10-12): Hybrid: NASA life-cycle gates with TRL/AD² for each critical technology, plus four discriminating gates (target, demand, economics, licence). Stringency follows reversibility.
- D-03 (proposed; treat as interim): Set an ALARP requirement with an interim design ceiling. The number itself goes to modelling, tests and the licensing state.
- D-04 (proposed; treat as interim): Use SEL1 as the reference case. Re-decide jointly with Phase 1 at the 0B gate.
- D-05 (proposed; treat as interim): Select no propellant yet. Cost iodine as the reference case and argon as the alternate, pending the supply audit and life tests. Water EP stays a desk study until a C-type target is confirmed.

Under D-02, KDP-0B (the one-way commitment to 0B production) needs every project-ending technology
at TRL 6 in a relevant environment with no waivers; internal 0A milestones need TRL 4–5.

### This item: bom-0-2 Mining Robots (0B (pathfinder units in 0A))
Accepted scope: Tether-powered excavation robots at the target NEA, with onboard batteries for mobility and safe mode, plus replacements.

Round-2 proposals for this item (per model; not approved as numbers):
- resize · bom-0-2 mining robots · supported by all · quantity: Claude 8 + 4 replacements; Gemini 20 (12 + 8); GPT 6 + 6 replacements · cost: Claude $30–80M; Gemini $35–55M; GPT $30–70M · confidence: low (Claude, GPT); medium (Gemini)

Critical technologies (TRL re-baseline, panel envelope):
- T04 Asteroid excavation (with anchoring per Gemini and GPT): TRL 2–3 now, target 6, AD² 6–7, project-ending
- T08 Particle containment, escape verification and tailings management: TRL 2–3 now, target 6, AD² 6–7, project-ending
- T09 High-voltage power tethers and site distribution on regolith: TRL 2–4 now, target 6, AD² 5–6, architecture-change
- T10 Long-duration autonomy for mining, processing and proximity operations: TRL 2–4 now, target 6, AD² 6, project-ending
- T16 Anchoring, hold-down and surface mobility on low-cohesion bodies: TRL 2–4 now, target 6, AD² 7, project-ending
- T21 Robotic maintenance, repair and spares logistics (GPT: and site installation and recovery): TRL 2–4 now, target 6, AD² 6, project-ending
- T24 Dust-tolerant long-life mechanisms and seals: TRL 2–5 now, target 6, AD² 5–6, project-ending

Other Phase 0 items (do not duplicate their scope): bom-0-1 Prospecting Survey and Rendezvous Scouts; bom-0-3 Processing Plant at the Target NEA; bom-0-4 MW-class Cargo Tugs; bom-0-5 Site Power, Arrays and Storage; bom-0-6 Water Pilot (C-type target only); bom-0-7 Organizational Infrastructure; bom-0-8 Earth-to-Space Launch and Delivery; bom-0-9 Communications and Ground Segment; bom-0-10 Mission Operations; bom-0-11 NRE, Ground R&D and Qualification; bom-0-12 0A Pathfinder Demonstrator; bom-0-13 Phase 1 Receiving Node (SEL1); bom-0-14 Spares and Replacements; bom-0-15 Debris and Contamination Control; bom-0-16 Electric-Propulsion Propellant Supply; bom-0-17 Contingency and Reserve.

State quantities and costs as ranges with their basis, split 0A and 0B where the item spans both,
and say where you disagree with the round-2 figures and why.

### Round-2 reconciliation for this item

# bom-0-2 Mining Robots: Phase-0 Round-2 Reconciliation

**Panel:** Claude Opus 5.5 ("Claude"), Gemini 3.8 Flash ("Gemini"), GPT-6.1 Sol ("GPT").
**Scope:** findings P0-F02, P0-F07 and P0-F14.

All values below are attributed to the model or models that stated them. The rapporteur adds no technical claims. Internal inconsistencies and labelling problems are listed in the final Reviewer note.

---

## 1. Verdict matrix

| Finding | Claude | Gemini | GPT |
|---|---|---|---|
| **P0-F02**: mining rate, robot target and station throughput disagree | agree | agree | **partly** |
| **P0-F07**: robot mass and power are inconsistent | agree | agree | **partly** |
| **P0-F14**: debris, contamination and regulation unbudgeted | agree | agree | agree |

**Where the panel stands**

- **P0-F02.** All three agree that the phase mass flow does not close. All three agree that a remote 50 kt/yr station cannot be fed through roughly 1 kt/yr of transport.
  - GPT's "partly" turns on one point: the hourly and annual figures can coexist at a 2.3–5.7% duty cycle, so they are not inherently contradictory.
  - Claude accepts that logic. It still calls an unstated 2–6% duty on a $50M asset a substantive gap.
- **P0-F07.** All three agree that the 500 kg reference is wrong. All three agree that the rq-0-26 torque figure (50–200 N·m at 10 kW) is physically incoherent.
  - Claude and Gemini judge 20–50 kW to be an overestimate.
  - GPT's "partly" holds that 20–50 kW is not intrinsically impossible on a 2.5–3.5 t robot. In GPT's view the power and restraint architecture is simply unclosed, so it keeps 20–50 kW as a test envelope.
- **P0-F14.** The panel is unanimous that the hazard is unbudgeted and that ">99% containment by mass" is inadequate. All three also agree that tailings dominate the residue stream. They disagree on the replacement metric and its value (see §3).

---

## 2. Agreed changes

These are supported by all three models unless a dissent or silence is noted.

| A2 | Withdraw the rq-0-26 torque basis (50–200 N·m at 10 kW). It implies roughly 480–1,900 rpm (Claude, GPT) or about 955 rpm at 100 N·m (Gemini) | Replacement torque values diverge (§3, D7) | All three |
| A3 | State an explicit excavation duty cycle in the spec, linking nameplate rate to annual output | Values diverge (§3, D4) | All three |
| A4 | Baseline on-robot physical beneficiation at about 1:1. Do not baseline magnetic or electrostatic beneficiation | ~1:1. Claude 1.0–1.3 (ref 1.1); Gemini 1.0–1.05; GPT ~1:1 with no credited gain. Combined envelope 1.0–1.3 | All three |

Escalate the station's location and role as a phase-level decision | — | All three. Claude strikes "Branch R" as failing a must. Gemini says bom-0-3 must be co-located or repurposed for volatiles. The project develops its own limits. bom-0-7 owns the assurance and authorisation work | — | All three. GPT explicitly rejects bom-0-7 "establishing international thresholds" |
| A16 | Withdraw round-1 "high confidence" ratings on excavation power, production and mass | — | Claude (withdraws Gemini's round-1 20 kW high confidence) and GPT (does not endorse round-1 high-confidence estimates). **Gemini dissents in effect:** it assigns high confidence to its own new 4 kW / 8 kW values (§3, D2) |

**Two-of-three agreements (third model silent)**

- **Design cutting life of 20,000+ h is not derived and should be tied to duty.** Claude gives 7,500 h (5,000–12,500). GPT gives about 11,000 h (5,000–21,000). Gemini is silent.
- **Dual bucket wheels should be a candidate, not a hard requirement.** Claude and GPT hold this. Gemini retains the wheel and does not address alternatives to it.

---

## 3. Preserved divergences

### D1. Fleet size and initial commitment

| Position | Held by | Reasoning |
|---|---|---|
| 3 pathfinders + up to 17 conditional. Branch W needs only 6–14 in total | Claude | Caps capital at risk at about $0.3–0.5B. Productivity is uncertain by 2–6×. It is likely (60–75%) that first-generation output falls ≥2× short |
| 2 pathfinders → 6 operational (range 2–8) | Gemini | 6 robots × 2,600 t/yr ≈ 15.6 kt/yr closes with co-located ISPP and about 1–2 kt/yr transport. This cuts recurring cost to $300–400M |
| 3 initial, 20 as a conditional ceiling | GPT | Buys flight learning before replication. Loss of one of three robots raises required duty to 17–71%, eliminating margin |

### D2. Excavation and electrical power

| Position | Held by | Reasoning |
|---|---|---|
| Mechanical 2 kW (0.5–5) including conveying; cutter sub-kW in fines. Electrical peak 7 kW (3–12). Test rig 10 kW and 10 kN·m stall per wheel | Claude | Specific energy of about 1–10× strength. Fines ≤1 kPa cohesion give 15–135 W at 0.15 m/s tip speed. Weak boulders need 1.4–7 kW at full cut depth. Power is not the binding constraint; anchoring and handling are |
| Mechanical 4 kW (2–8). Electrical 8 kW (5–12). **High confidence** | Gemini | Specific energy 0.05–0.5 kWh/t. Clast grinding at about 2 kWh/t keeps cutting under about 5 kW. 20–50 kW reflects terrestrial hard-rock metrics |
| Mechanical 20–50 kW retained as a two-wheel **test envelope**. Electrical 25–70 kW. Low confidence | GPT | Surface-contact heritage does not establish specific energy. Competent inclusions may need much more. The lower 2–10 kW "may be appropriate for some loose material" but is a hypothesis to measure |

### D3. Power source architecture

| Position | Held by | Reasoning |
|---|---|---|
| Own arrays (20–50 m², ref 35) + 15–40 kWh battery, recharged at a hub. Umbilical ≤300 m is a production option. Beamed power rejected | Claude | Pathfinders on uncharacterised boulder fields should not depend on cabling with unknown snag or abrasion behaviour |
| Small housekeeping array (15–25 m², 3–5 kW) + 30–50 kWh battery as pathfinder baseline (DQ decision and YAML). Umbilical (1–3 kV DC) as growth path. The spec table instead lists "tethered umbilical + buffer" as primary, high confidence | Gemini | Large arrays on a walking robot create inertial coupling, snagging and attitude problems. See Reviewer note on the internal inconsistency |
| Fixed anchored site power node with managed cable/docking. Robots work within a bounded area, not unrestricted walking. Battery 10–30 kWh for safing only | GPT | At 25–70 kW, 8 h of battery operation needs 200–560 kWh (1.1–4.7 t). Tethers are not inherently unacceptable, but unrestricted tethered walking is a poor baseline |

All three label this a **trade-off point**: autonomy and mobility versus mass, power and dust exposure.

### D4. Dig rate, duty cycle and per-robot output

| Parameter | Claude | Gemini | GPT |
|---|---|---|---|
| Nameplate rate | 2 t/h (1–3) in fines; 0.3 t/h (0.1–0.5) in weak-boulder comminution | 2.0 t/h (1.5–3.5) | 2–5 t/h, as a test objective only |
| Duty / cutting hours | 1,500 h/yr (1,000–2,500) | 15% (10–25%), about 1,300 h/yr | 25% reference (11–48%) for three robots |
| Output | 3,000 t/yr per robot (1,000–7,500) | 2,600 t/yr per robot (1,800–3,500) | 15–25 kt/yr fleet total (ref 20) from three robots |
| Rate-limiting factor | Anchoring and handling (ACH, see §6) | Not stated | Not asserted; six-axis loads must be measured |

### D5. Robot dry mass

- **Claude:** 2,500 kg (1,600–4,000), from a bottom-up budget including 20–30% margin.
- **Gemini:** 2,800 kg (2,400–3,200), from a subsystem build-up (no table given).
- **GPT:** 3,000–5,000 kg landed. This is a reserve allocation, excludes detached site infrastructure, and "is not evidence that lighter robots cannot work".

### D6. Battery and night operation

- **Claude:** 15–40 kWh. Night digging only on fast rotators, at 3–5 kW for 2–4 h, needing 6–20 kWh.
- **Gemini:** 30–50 kWh buffer. Continuous night digging would need "several tonnes" of battery per robot.
- **GPT:** 10–30 kWh, safing only. Night-side excavation from robot batteries is not to be baselined.

### D7. Reaction torque and cancellation

- **Claude:** 0.1–1 kN·m per wheel in fines, with a 5 kN·m stall rating. Uncancelled crowd force is 30–900 N in fines and ≤2 kN in boulder mode. The "90–95% cancellation" figure has no supporting test or DEM result (very low confidence).
- **Gemini:** about 1,000 N·m per wheel at 2 kW and 2 rad/s. Counter-rotation cancels 90–95%, leaving a residual of 75 N·m (25–150).
- **GPT:** illustratively 2–25 kN·m per wheel at 20–50 kW and 1–5 rad/s. Cancellation is credited only when demonstrated. GPT requires a measured six-axis load envelope.

### D8. Containment metric and limits

| Position | Held by | Reasoning |
|---|---|---|
| Three-part requirement: (a) all external handling velocities ≤0.5 v_esc; (b) deposition ≤0.1 g/m²/yr of <100 µm dust at protected surfaces; (c) site escape ≤1 t/yr (0.1–10). Mass fraction is "the wrong control variable" | Claude | Escape is governed by velocity and harm by deposition flux. 99.9995% from a seal on an open face is not verifiable. Escaped fine grains are cleared by radiation pressure and P-R drag. Claude states explicitly that its budget is looser than GPT's |
| ≤10 kg/robot/yr (≥99.99%; range 99.95–99.999%), ≤60–100 kg/yr fleet. Tip speed ≤0.2 m/s. Electrostatic curtains | Gemini | >99.999% is infeasible because of seal abrasion; 99.99% balances seal life against <0.5%/yr array degradation |
| 10–100 kg/yr site-wide uncontrolled release across all handling stages (≈99.9995–99.99995% at 20 kt/yr). Receiver limit ≤1%/yr performance loss. Automatic stop rules | GPT | A provisional risk allocation that "may prove impractical". Accounting must cover particle size, velocity and destination, not mass alone |

**Velocity limit**

- Claude makes the limit relative to the body: 0.5 v_esc, i.e. 0.02–0.2 m/s.
- Gemini fixes it at ≤0.2 m/s.
- GPT sets no tip-speed limit.

### D9. Fate of fugitive dust

- **Claude:** at ≤0.5 v_esc, most fugitive grains stay bound and fall back, so the hazard is local redeposition. Electrostatic lofting is an uncertain exception. Claude calls Gemini's round-1 "inevitably exceeds escape velocity" incorrect as a design statement.
- **Gemini (F14 reasoning):** tool tip speeds of 0.5–2.0 m/s exceed v_esc, so 600+ t/yr becomes orbital and heliocentric debris. (Its own proposal sets ≤0.2 m/s; see Reviewer note.)
- **GPT:** neither "most grains fall back" nor "particles inevitably escape" is supported without particle-release distributions. Escape does not imply leaving the operating environment.

### D10. Excavated-material temperature rise

- **Claude:** about 4 K (2–15 K) at 2 kW. Thermal isolation becomes a verification item only.
- **GPT:** round-1's blanket 5–15 K "is not defensible". At 20–50 kW with all energy entering the feed, the rise is 14–130 K, and partitioning must be measured.
- **Gemini:** silent.

This divergence follows from D2.

### D11. Water yield, export and station feed

| | Claude | Gemini | GPT |
|---|---|---|---|
| Water assumption | 3–8 wt% recoverable × 70–90% recovery | 5–10 wt% H₂O in CI/CM | 5 wt% × 80% |
| Exported | 250–1,000 t/yr | 1,200 t/yr (800–2,000) to bom-0-4 | 700 t/yr (450–950) |
| bom-0-3 feed | 0 directly (Branch W); 47–62 kt/yr dried feed if co-located (Branch C) | 0 t/yr (0–1,000) | 450–950 t/yr water; bom-0-3 re-scoped as a water-conditioning service |
| Transport ceiling | ~1 kt/yr, unverified (P0-F01) | 1–2 kt/yr, "physically bounded by Kr/I electric propulsion" | ~1 kt/yr, provisional and unverified |

### D12. Mobility concept

- **Claude:** walking robot, with arrays stowed near the face and while walking.
- **Gemini:** raises an anchored gantry or tether frame with winch traversal as an alternative to walking hexapods or rovers.
- **GPT:** robots excavate docked or tethered within a bounded work area.

### D13. Excavation mechanism

- **Claude:** whether bucket wheels or drums suit the target at all is "about as likely as not (40–60%), low confidence". Percussive crushing, bagging or a drag-line may suit boulder-dominated sites better.
- **GPT:** opposed drums, enclosed coring and restrained collection remain credible competitors.
- **Gemini:** retains the bucket wheel. It flags stall and shock torque on competent (>50 MPa) inclusions.

### D14. Evidence readings

- **Grott et al. (2019):**
  - Claude cites it for boulder tensile strength of about 200–280 kPa.
  - GPT reads it as a low-conductivity, high-porosity result and "not a direct industrial excavation-strength measurement".
  - Gemini cites it for micro-compressive strength below 1 MPa.
- **Near-surface cohesion:** Claude ≤1 kPa (Arakawa 2020); Gemini 0.1–10 Pa.

### D15. Interface values (non-exhaustive)

- **Power to bom-0-5:**
  - Claude: fleet average 20–80 kW, peak ≤0.2 MW.
  - Gemini: 60 kW (30–100).
  - GPT: 0.075–0.21 MW cutting and a 0.1–0.3 MW reserve. GPT separately flags 0.5–2 MW site demand for ISPP heating.
- **Data:**
  - Claude: 0.1–1 Mbps per robot on site; 0.1–2 Mbps aggregate to Earth.
  - Gemini: 100 kbps to bom-0-7.
  - GPT: 1–10 GB/day per active robot.
- **Robot propellant:** Claude 0.2–1 t/yr fleet; GPT 0.01–0.10 t/yr; Gemini none stated.
- **"in_bom" flags differ:**
  - Claude marks the bom-0-5 power and bom-0-6 mass interfaces as not in the BOM.
  - GPT marks both as in the BOM, but marks cables and docking as not in it.

### D16. Regulatory specifics

- **Claude:** COSPAR planetary-protection category for an NEA mining site is most likely Category II. Earth return has precedent as "unrestricted". US operators face a mission-authorisation gap. Candidate domiciles: Luxembourg, UAE, Japan.
- **Gemini:** names the US Commercial Space Launch Competitiveness Act and the Luxembourg Space Resources Act.
- **GPT:** COSPAR, ITU and debris standards are not interchangeable. No claim on the national pathway should be made without jurisdiction-specific legal review.

### D17. Programme cost

- **Claude:** total about $2.1–5.5B against the $1.0B line. It is likely (≥80%) to exceed $2B, at medium confidence.
- **GPT:** mining-campaign subtotal for three robots is $0.9–2.5B. This excludes shared ISPP, generation, transport, prospecting and station, so it is not a phase total.
- **Gemini:** no roll-up. Recurring cost falls to $300–400M.

## 5. Open questions

# bom-0-2 Mining Robots: Technical Proposal

**Item:** bom-0-2 Mining Robots. Pathfinder units in 0A; production fleet in gated 0B.
**Baseline context:** Fe-Ni product co-located at the target NEA; SEL1 reference receiving node (D-04, interim); robots tether-powered from site power.
**Status:** Proposal for configuration control. All numbers are ranges with a stated basis. Confidence is stated per number. Nothing here is adopted until the owner accepts it.

---

## 0. Executive summary

I recommend a robot concept called the **Anchored Cell Excavator (ACE)**. Its main features:

- **Body and mobility.** It is a low, wide, wheel-less sled. It moves as a cable-driven parallel robot inside a pre-anchored work cell of about 30 m, using four on-board winches on four anchor lines.
- **Power.** It is fed by a ±1 kV DC bipolar tether (2 kV pole-to-pole) from a cell power node supplied under bom-0-5.
- **Excavation.** It collects fines with an enclosed pair of slow, counter-rotating, up-cut drums. The drums are arranged so their steady reaction pulls the head into the material rather than pushing the robot off the body.
- **Cobbles.** A second manipulator with a grab clears cobbles and services anchors and other robots.

The design follows five principles.

1. **On a rubble pile you cannot push on the ground.** The robot weighs about 0.1–0.5 N on a Bennu- or Itokawa-class body. At milli-g, digging is a load-path problem, not a power problem.
   - Every steady force must close inside the robot–material system.
   - Anchors must carry only pretension and bounded transients.
   - Slip clutches must cap transients below the anchor capacity actually demonstrated.
2. **Collect, don't mine.** The robot takes the <25 mm fines fraction at about 1:1 (per A4) and does no comminution. Competent ordinary-chondrite clasts are pushed aside, not cut.
   - This puts baseline electrical demand at about 2.5 kW average and 8 kW peak, not tens of kW.
3. **Size for the actual product.** Round 2 sized the fleet for a water-first chain. The binding baseline is native and reduced Fe-Ni, so the excavated tonnage is set by **metal grade × recovery**.
   - At 1.3 kt/yr product, 10 wt% metal and 60% recovery, the robots must deliver about **22 kt/yr** of run-of-mine fines.
4. **Nothing the robot does may exceed 0.25–0.3 v_esc.** This applies to the robot body and to anything the robot touches.
   - A robot that loses every anchor at maximum speed therefore stays gravitationally bound and recoverable.
   - Material the robot handles cannot be launched to escape by the robot's own kinematics.
5. **Buy evidence before replicas.**
   - 0A: two flight pathfinders, plus one ground qualification model under bom-0-11.
   - 0B: a fleet sized at KDP-0B from signed Phase 1 demand and measured pathfinder productivity. Reference: 8 delivered (6 active + 2 spare/servicing) and 3 later replacements.

**Cost (bom-0-2 recurring hardware only; low confidence):**

| | Range | Reference |
|---|---|---|
| 0A | $120–245M | $170M |
| 0B (gated) | $345–730M | $500M |

Robot-specific NRE is $300–650M (ref $450M) and is carried in **bom-0-11**, not here.

**Where I depart from the round-2 panel:**

- Fleet basis: Fe-Ni rather than water.
- Power: reject 25–70 kW as baseline.
- Mobility: reject walking and bucket wheels.
- Pathfinders: 2 rather than 3.
- Duty cycle: higher in 0B, lower in 0A.
- Velocity rule: tighter and body-relative.
- Test rig: no 10 kN·m stall rig.

Details are in §11.

---

## 1. What changes when the binding context is applied

| Driver | Round-2 assumption | Binding context | Consequence for robots |
|---|---|---|---|
| Product | Water-first (Claude W, GPT, Gemini) | Native/reduced Fe-Ni; water only as a C-type pilot (bom-0-6) | Tonnage is set by metal grade × recovery, not water wt% |
| Plant location | Disputed | Co-located at the target NEA | Short haul (≤50 m) to a sealed dock; no on-robot beneficiation |
| Power | Arrays vs tether disputed | HV tether, 1–3 kV, 10–50 kWh battery | Arrays on the robot are deleted. The robot is sized round tether and anchors |
| Delivered product | — | 0.6–2.5 kt/yr | Fleet range 3–16 robots across the full envelope (§3) |
| Crew | — | Uncrewed | Peer robotic servicing is a design driver (T21) |

---

## 2. Physical environment the design is built round

| Parameter | Design range | Basis / note |
|---|---|---|
| Body diameter | 0.3–1.5 km rubble pile | Typical accessible S-type NEA. Fe-Ni favours H/L-chondrite-like S-types |
| Surface gravity | 2×10⁻⁵ to 3×10⁻⁴ m/s² | Itokawa about 1×10⁻⁴; Bennu about 6×10⁻⁵ |
| Escape velocity | 0.15–0.6 m/s | Itokawa about 0.17 m/s; Bennu about 0.2 m/s; a 1 km S-type about 0.5 m/s |
| Robot weight on surface (2.65 t) | 0.05–0.8 N | Weight is negligible. Every load path is anchor- or inertia-limited |
| Surface-layer cohesion | 0–10 Pa design; up to 1 kPa at depth (unknown) | Gravity-regime cratering on Ryugu and very low resistance at Bennu TAG imply a near-cohesionless top layer. I side with Gemini's 0.1–10 Pa for the top 0.3 m, and design for Claude's ≤1 kPa only as an upper bound at depth |
| Fines (<25 mm) fraction in selected ponds | ≥60% by mass required | **Target-selection requirement, not an assumption.** Pushed to bom-0-1 and the target gate |
| Free metal in fines | 8–18 wt% acceptable; 10 wt% reference | H-chondrite-like. LL-like (about 2 wt%) targets do not close (§3) |
| Surface temperature | 200–400 K diurnal | About 1 AU; equator and mid-latitudes |
| Rotation period | 4–12 h | Night lasts 2–6 h. The tether lets robots work through night on site storage |
| Mid-latitude effective gravity | Must be >0 at site | Rules out near-critical equators on fast rotators. Site-selection requirement |

**The governing number.** A 50 N crowd force applied for 30 s to a free 2.65 t robot gives Δv ≈ 0.57 m/s, which exceeds escape velocity on every candidate. No design that relies on robot mass or ground bearing can work. Hence principle 1.

---

## 3. Fleet sizing for the Fe-Ni product

### 3.1 Excavation demand

M_exc = P / (g_m × η_r)

- P = delivered Fe-Ni product
- g_m = free-metal grade in the robot-delivered fines
- η_r = plant recovery to product specification (bom-0-3 owns this; I use it only for sizing)

| Case | P (kt/yr) | g_m | η_r | Yield | M_exc (kt/yr) |
|---|---|---|---|---|---|
| Low demand, rich target | 0.6 | 18% | 80% | 14.4% | 4.2 |
| **Reference** | **1.3** | **10%** | **60%** | **6.0%** | **22** |
| High demand, reference target | 2.5 | 10% | 60% | 6.0% | 42 |
| Reference demand, lean target | 1.3 | 5% | 50% | 2.5% | 52 |
| LL-like target (reject) | 1.3 | 2% | 60% | 1.2% | 108 |

The reference tailings stream is about 21 kt/yr. This is consistent with GPT's 19.2 kt/yr (14–24 kt/yr).

### 3.2 Per-robot output

| Factor | 0A pathfinder (yr 1) | 0B reference | 0B range | Basis |
|---|---|---|---|---|
| Nameplate dig rate in fines | 1–2 t/h | 2.0 t/h | 1–3 t/h | §5.3: 2 drums × 0.6 m × 5 cm × 7 mm/s × 1.3 t/m³ ≈ 2 t/h |
| Fraction of an active hour spent digging | 0.4 | 0.6 | 0.5–0.7 | Hopper fill about 45 min, then about 25 min to dock and return |
| Availability (servicing, re-rigging, holds, faults) | 0.15–0.25 | 0.40 | 0.25–0.55 | Tethered, so not illumination-limited. Rigging is about 5% |
| Cutting hours per year | 400–1,000 | **2,000** | 1,000–3,000 | 8,760 × availability × dig fraction |
| Output per robot | 0.4–2 kt/yr | **4.0 kt/yr** | 1.0–7.5 kt/yr | — |

My 0B figure is above Claude's 1,500 h and Gemini's 1,300 h, for one reason. Under the binding tether-plus-site-storage architecture, robots are not illumination-limited. The 2–6 h nights on 4–12 h rotators are covered by site storage at about 20 kW fleet load: 40–120 kWh per night, against 0.5–15 MWh of site storage.

My 0A figure is deliberately low. First-flight robots spend most of their time on characterisation, not production.

### 3.3 Fleet

N_active = ⌈M_exc / O_robot⌉
N_delivered = N_active + ⌈0.33 × N_active⌉ (servicing rotation and peer-repair spares)

| Case | M_exc | N_active (at 4 kt/yr) | N_delivered | Replacements (5 yr) | Total 0B units |
|---|---|---|---|---|---|
| Low | 4.2 | 2 | 3 | 1 | 4 |
| **Reference** | **22** | **6** | **8** | **3** | **11** |
| High | 42 | 11 | 14 | 4 | 18 (exceeds the 16 I would authorise; re-plan) |
| Lean target | 52 | 13 | 17 | 5 | Fails the economics gate; re-target |

**Replacements are derived from reliability, not forecast.** I side with GPT here.

- Reference loads: 6 active robots × 5 yr × about 4,000 operating h = 120,000 robot-hours.
- Target mission-ending failure rate after peer repair: 1 per 40,000 h. That gives about 3 losses.
- The range of 2–5 corresponds to an unrecoverable MTBF of 25,000–60,000 h.
- The bom-0-14 depot covers recoverable failures through LRU swaps.

**Recommendation.** Authorise 0B at the reference size of 8 + 3 only if the pathfinders demonstrate the KDP-0B productivity floor in §8.4. The final N is fixed at the gate under D-01.

---

## 4. Work-cell architecture

```
                      SITE PLAN (one active work cell, ~30 m across)

           A1 (boulder sling, >=2 m clast)              A2 (screw-umbrella pile)
             o------------------------------------------o
             |\                                        /|
             | \  anchor line L1         anchor line L2/ |
             |  \                                    /  |
             |   \        BENCH (unexcavated)       /   |
             |    \     +--------------------+     /    |
             |     \    |   ACE robot (sled) |    /     |       CPN = cell power node (bom-0-5)
             |      +===|  4 winches  [hopper]|===+      |       SD  = sealed dock (bom-0-3 inlet)
             |          +---------+----------+          |       ~~~ = HV/fibre tether (on robot reel)
             |                    | boom (4.5 m)        |
             |       .............v.............        |
             |       :  PAN (excavated, 0-1.5 m) :      |
             |       :   drum head works face   :       |
             |       :..........................:       |
             |      /                          \        |
             |     / L4                      L3 \       |
             o----/------------------------------\-----o
           A4  [SD]~~~~~~~~~~~~~~~~~~~~~~~~~~~~~~~~[CPN]  A3
                 ^ sealed dock inside the anchor web, so the robot reaches it on its own lines

      Site guide-line network (fixed lines) links cells, the dock and the hub for inter-cell moves.
```

**How the cell works.**

- **Cell rigging.** Four perimeter anchors, A1–A4, sit 12–18 m from the cell centre.
  - Boulder slings (straps round embedded clasts ≥2 m) are the bootstrap type. They need manipulation only, no driving force.
  - Once two slings hold, the robot can react the torque of driving screw-umbrella piles against them.
- **Mobility.** The robot moves as a cable-driven parallel robot: four winches pay out and haul in four anchor lines. There are no wheels and no legs.
  - Speed limit is ≤0.25 v_esc of the body, i.e. 0.04–0.15 m/s.
  - Line pretension is 30–80 N.
- **Benching.** The robot sits on an unexcavated bench at anchor elevation and reaches down into the pan with its boom.
  - It never digs under itself. Otherwise the lines would angle upward and lift it.
  - One bench pass covers about 20 m × 6 m × 1.5 m ≈ 230 t, taking about 2–3 weeks.
  - One cell level holds about 1,400 t, i.e. about 3–4 months per robot.
  - The robot then re-rigs to the next level or cell.
- **Hopper cycle.** The robot travels on its own lines to the sealed dock inside the web and transfers through a double-door port, then returns. A dock sits ≤20 m from any working point.
- **Inter-cell moves** use fixed guide lines installed during site build. During site build the robots themselves rig the lines (T21 site installation).

**Why not walking or wheels.** Traction is proportional to weight, and weight is effectively zero.

- Walking hexapods with microspines need a grip capacity on rubble that nobody has demonstrated. They also add 12–18 actuated joints, each exposed to dust (T24).
- Cable-driven mobility puts all motion actuators inside the sealed body and makes every force on the robot a measured line tension.

---

## 5. The robot (ACE-1)

### 5.1 General arrangement

```

        radiator (edge-on to Sun, 2 x 3 m², EDS-coated)

        [o]======||==========================\\
   +---------------------------------------------+      tether reel (350 m) + level-wind
   | avionics | battery 30 kWh | PMAD +/-1 kV   |~~~~~~~~~~~~~~~~~~~~~~~~ to CPN
   |----------+----------------+-------------- |
   | W1  W2 (winches)     HOPPER 1.2 m³  W3  W4 |----- anchor lines L1..L4
   |          [alpha-beta transfer port]       |
   +==================SKID (3.0 x 2.4 m)========+
   ////////////////// BENCH /////////////////// \
                                                \  boom (3-DOF, 4.5 m reach)
                                                 \
                                            +-----\------+
                                            | HOOD + brush|
                                            |  skirt      |
                                            | (D1)  (D2)  |  <- counter-rotating up-cut drums
                                            +-------------+     0.5 m dia x 0.6 m wide each

```

### 5.2 Principal specifications

| Dry mass, CBE | 2,130 kg | — | Low-medium | §5.8 bottom-up |
| Dry mass, MEV (25% margin) | 2,650 kg | Allocation 1,800–3,500 kg | Low-medium | Margin per early-concept practice |
| Stowed envelope | 3.0 × 2.4 × 1.3 m | — | Medium | Two units stack in a 5 m fairing; fits a bom-0-4 payload bay |
| Footprint (skid) | 3.0 × 2.4 m | — | Medium | — |
| Boom reach | 4.5 m | 3.5–5.5 m | Medium | Sets the 6 m swath and 1.5 m pan depth |
| Design life | 5 yr surface | 15,000 operating h; 10,000 cutting h with LRU swaps | Low | Drives, structure and PMAD |
| Head wear-LRU interval | 2,000 cutting h | 1,000–3,000 h | Low | Abrasive test is a pre-replication gate |
| Seal LRU interval | 1,500 h | 500–3,000 h | Low | T24 |
| Max body speed | 0.25 v_esc | Absolute 0.04–0.15 m/s | High (it is a rule) | Bound-on-detachment safety rule |
| Max tool-imparted particle speed | 0.3 v_esc | Absolute 0.05–0.18 m/s | High (rule); verification low | §7 |
| Nameplate dig rate (fines) | 2.0 t/h | 1–3 t/h | Low | §5.3 |
| Output per active robot | 4.0 kt/yr | 1.0–7.5 kt/yr | Low | §3.2 |
| On-board beneficiation | None (1:1) | 1.0–1.3 incidental from the grizzly | Medium | A4 |

### 5.3 Excavation head

| Item | Specification |

| Type | Enclosed counter-rotating drum pair (RASSOR lineage), **up-cut geometry** |
| Drums | 0.50 m diameter × 0.60 m wide each; 12 scoops each; 25 mm grizzly bars across scoop mouths |
| Speed | ≤2.0 rpm (ω ≈ 0.2 rad/s), giving tip speed ≤0.05 m/s on a 0.17 m/s body. The speed is scheduled to the measured v_esc of the target |

| Electrical, head, peak | 2 kW (jam reverse and clear) |
| Hood | Rigid enclosure. Brush and labyrinth skirt, 50 mm compliant stroke. Electrodynamic dust shield (EDS) on the window and sensor ports |
| Instrumentation | Six-axis F/T at the boom wrist; drum torque and speed; hood-internal particle imager; skirt-gap lidar |

**Why up-cut.** In the contact zone the scoops move upward and inward through the material. Material drag on the scoops therefore points down, so the head is *pulled into* the face.

- The boom holds the head back in tension.
- The reaction enters the robot as compression onto the skid and bench, not as uplift on the anchors.
- The two drums' horizontal components oppose each other.

**I do not credit any cancellation fraction (contra Gemini's 90–95%).** The residual six-axis load is a measured quantity. It is the T04 exit metric.

**What the head does not do.**

- It does not cut competent clasts. Ordinary-chondrite cobbles are tens to hundreds of MPa in strength, and cutting them would need multi-kW power and kN·m torques that no demonstrated anchor can react.
- The grizzly rejects anything over 25 mm. Cobbles of 25–400 mm (≤150 kg) are cleared by the grab into a windrow at the cell edge.
- Collection of cobbles for a plant crusher is a bom-0-3 decision. The grab and hopper can support it at about 0.5 t/h.

**Carried alternates (decided at the 0A downselect, §8):**

- **H-alt-1: sealed clamshell grab as primary collector.** Batch operation. Better containment and jam tolerance; lower rate, about 1–1.5 t/h.
- **H-alt-2: percussive comminution head** for boulder-dominated sites, at 5–10 kW. Only if the target gate forces it. The PMAD and tether already carry 15 kW for this reason.
- **Research only, not baselined (per A4): magnetic pick-up head.** Native Fe-Ni is ferromagnetic, so this is a potential beneficiation multiplier. It is tested on the pathfinder as an experiment.

## 7. Containment (T08): robot-side allocation

bom-0-15 owns the site requirement and the ALARP ceiling (D-03). bom-0-2 proposes the following robot allocation, which uses velocity and enclosure as the verifiable controls.

| ID | Requirement | Value | Verification |
|---|---|---|---|
| MR-C1 | Tool-imparted particle velocity | ≤0.3 v_esc of the target, for all robot motions | Drop-tower and parabolic DEM validation; high-speed imaging in the pathfinder hood |
| MR-C2 | Body speed | ≤0.25 v_esc | Flight software limit, independently monitored |
| MR-C3 | Release outside the hood or hopper envelope, <1 mm grains, any velocity | ≤10 kg per robot per yr design goal (≈2.5 ppm of 4 kt/yr) | Witness plates, hood-skirt imager, mass balance (hopper vs dock) |
| MR-C4 | Release outside the envelope at >0.5 v_esc | ≤1 kg per robot per yr design goal | Inferred from MR-C1 and C3 distributions; witness-plate trajectory reconstruction |
| MR-C5 | Transfer-port release per dock cycle | ≤5 g | Vacuum-chamber cycle tests (≥2,000 cycles) |
| MR-C6 | Automatic stop rules | Stop the head when a hood-skirt gap exceeds 20 mm, a particle-imager count exceeds threshold, or a bom-0-15 site monitor alarms | Pathfinder |

**Reasoning.**

- I adopt Claude's position that mass fraction is the wrong governing variable.
- I tighten Claude's 0.5 v_esc to **0.3 v_esc for robot-imparted velocity**, because the plant and dock will add their own release mechanisms and need headroom.
- I reject Gemini's fixed 0.2 m/s. It roughly equals v_esc on Bennu-class bodies, so as a fixed number it protects nothing.
- MR-C3 and MR-C4 are allocations for bom-0-15, not standards. The ceiling itself goes to modelling and to the licensing state.

**Tailings.** Robots do not own tailings. The ACE hopper and port are, however, reversible: a robot can take a tailings load at the dock and place it in a mined-out pan as backfill. At the reference 21 kt/yr this needs about 5,000 robot-h/yr, equal to +2 robots ($56–120M). **I offer this to bom-0-15 as a priced option, not baselined scope.**

**Two flight pathfinders (PF-1, PF-2), plus one QM on the ground (bom-0-11).** Not three flight units.

## 13. Manufacturing considerations

- **Volume.** 2 pathfinders, 1 QM, 1 EDU, and 4–16 production units. This is small-batch aerospace integration, not series manufacturing.
  - Production units are built in two lots: initial and replacements.
  - Line restart costs ($20–40M) are explicit.
- **Commonality.**
  - One LRU set is used fleet-wide: head, battery, reel, winch modules, avionics boxes.
  - Pathfinder and 0B units share primary structure. Configuration changes after KDP-0B are limited to LRUs where possible, so pathfinders can be upgraded in situ by peer swap.
- **Materials.**
  - Drum scoop liners: WC-Co hard-facing on a tough steel substrate.
  - Seals: PTFE-filled labyrinths with sacrificial brush stages.
  - Gear-heads: sealed and bellows-protected, with dry-film lubrication (sputtered MoS₂) where dust ingress is possible.
  - No wet lubricants are exposed to dust.
- **Dust-tolerant assembly.** No exposed sliding interfaces outside sealed modules. All connectors are robotic blind-mate types with dust doors.
- **Supply chain.**
  - Long-lead items: rad-tolerant processors, space-qualified Li-ion cells, HV DC-DC modules, aramid and Vectran lines.
  - Second sources are identified at PDR.
- **Phase 1 hook.** Wear parts (liners, scoops, anchor flukes) are specified to be makeable from on-site Fe-Ni once bom-0-3 product exists. This is a design-for-local-manufacture requirement on geometry and tolerances, not a Phase 0 commitment.
